Two pounds of chuck, one pound of pork. Trick number two, throw away the can of dry breadcrumbs. This is the thing that ruins more meatloaf than anything except lean beef. Dry crumbs are like a sponge that's already dry. They go into the meat and they soak up the juice from the meat itself. So your meatloaf ends up drier than it was before you added them. The old way is called a panade. Fancy word, simple thing. Take three slices of plain white sandwich bread, the cheap soft kind. Tear off the crusts, tear the bread into little pieces and put it in the bottom of your big mixing bowl. Pour in two-thirds of a cup of whole milk, mash it with a fork and let it sit 10 minutes until it turns into a soft paste like oatmeal. Here's what that paste does. The wet bread gets in between the little pieces of meat and it keeps the proteins from grabbing each other too tight while it bakes.

and it holds the milk inside the loaf. Instead of stealing the juice, the bread is adding juice. My father used day-old bread from the bakery next door. Any soft bread works. Three slices and two-thirds of a cup of milk for three pounds of meat. Trick number three, cook the onion first. Everybody chops a raw onion and throws it straight into the meat. And here's what happens. Raw onion is mostly water. Those chunks steam inside the loaf. They leave little holes. The loaf cracks right along them and you get a hard crunchy bite of half raw onion in a soft piece of meat. So take one big yellow onion and chop it fine, small as a pea. Put a tablespoon of butter in a pan on medium heat and cook the onion slowly, about eight minutes, until it's soft and see-through and just starting to turn gold. Add two cloves of garlic, chopped for the last minute.

Then take it off the heat and let it cool on a plate. It has to be cool before it touches the meat or it starts cooking the fat. While the pan is still warm, there's one more old shop trick. Put two tablespoons of ketchup, one tablespoon of Worcestershire sauce, and a spoon of mustard right in with the onion. Stir it for 30 seconds. That cooks the raw taste out. And that little bit of sweet and sour goes all the way through the meat. That's the taste people can't put their finger on. Trick number four. Mix it with your fingertips, not your fists. In the bowl, you've got the bread paste. Add two eggs, not four, and beat them right into the paste. Add the cool onion. Now is the time to fix it, not after it's baked. It takes two minutes, and you'll never serve a flat meatloaf again. Trick number five, the one that starts the argument. Get rid of the loaf pan. I know, your grandmother used a loaf pan, and her mother before her. But here's what actually happens in that pan. The fat melts out and has nowhere to go. So the bottom and the sides of the meatloaf sit in hot grease for an hour. They boil. That's why the sides are gray and soggy and the middle is dry. The old shop way is to shape it by hand, right on a baking sheet. Line the sheet with foil, put the meat in the middle, and shape it with wet hands into a loaf about 9 inches long, 5 inches wide, and 2 1⁄2 inches tall. flat on top, rounded on the edges. Wet hands keep the meat from sticking and they make the outside smooth so it doesn't crack.

Now the fat runs off onto the sheet and the heat touches every side of the loaf. The outside gets a brown crust all the way around, top and sides, not just the top. And here's an old trick my mother used. She'd lay two slices of bread on the sheet right under each end of the loaf. They soak up the grease and the dog got them after dinner. Trick number six, low and slow and trust the number, not the clock. Set the oven to 350 degrees, not 400. When the oven's too hot, the outside cooks hard and shrinks before the middle is done and it squeezes the juice out on its way. A three-pound meatloaf at 350 takes about an hour, maybe an hour and ten minutes, but every oven is different, so you don't trust the clock. you use a thermometer push it into the very center of the loaf from the side ground meat is done at 160 degrees

That's the number, 160 in the middle, and it's done. The school nurse baked hers for an hour and a half without a thermometer. By then, the middle was way past 180. Every degree past 160 is juice going into the pan. A little thermometer from the hardware store costs less than one pound of meat, and it'll save you a dry dinner every week for the rest of your life. Trick number seven, glaze it late and let it rest. Everybody puts the ketchup on top at the start. And after an hour in the oven, that sugar burns black and bitter. The glaze goes on in the last 15 minutes. Here's our shop glaze from the 70s. Half a cup of ketchup, two tablespoons of brown sugar, and one tablespoon of cider vinegar. Stir it in a cup.

When the thermometer says about 145, take the meatloaf out, spread the glaze thick over the top and down the sides, and put it back in the oven until the middle hits 160. The glaze bubbles, it gets sticky and shiny, and it's done right when the meat is. And then the hardest part. Leave it alone for 15 minutes. Don't cut it. I know everybody's standing there with a plate, but right out of the oven, the juice inside is moving around like water, and if you cut it now, it runs out all over the board, and the slices fall apart. After 15 minutes, the juice settles back into the meat, and it slices clean and thick, and every slice shines like the one I showed you at the start. Now, if something went wrong, here's what it means. If your meatloaf fell apart into crumbs, one of three things happened.

You used lean beef, you used dry crumbs instead of the bread paste, or you cut it hot. Next time, 80-20 chuck, the milk and bread, and 15 minutes on the board. If it came out dry, it was overcooked. Every time, it went past 160 in the middle, or the oven was too hot. That's the thermometer's job. And tonight, the fix is a little warm beef broth or pan gravy, spooned over the slices. If it came out tight and rubbery, like a sausage, it was mixed too much. Fingertips, one minute and stop. If it's greasy and gray on the sides, it was the loaf pan. Use the baking sheet, and if the top cracked wide open, there was raw onion in it, or the meat was mixed too dry, or the shape was too tall.
